title: Align CBPP Phase-2 Nelder-Mead with lme4 stage-2 conventions
description:
## Why
Profiling under interlace-1yyz showed CBPP fit time is dominated by the
Phase-2 Nelder-Mead refinement in glmm_laplace.py:1548 (~93% of CBPP
wall time, 403 evals at maxiter=2000, xatol/fatol=1e-7, adaptive=True).

Initial framing of this issue suggested skipping Phase 2 entirely or
capping maxiter aggressively. After comparing with lme4 source and
running lme4 empirically on CBPP, that framing was wrong:

- lme4 ALWAYS runs both stages (R/lmer.R:154-198, R/modular.R:911).
  Stage 1 = bobyqa over theta (beta profiled), Stage 2 = Nelder-Mead
  over (theta, beta) jointly. Skipping stage 2 would diverge from
  lme4 with no clear correctness story for harder GLMMs (zero-inflated,
  observation-level RE).

- lme4 on CBPP empirically: Nelder-Mead, 285 stage-2 evals, ~115ms
  median wall on this host. interlace: 403 evals, 682ms. Eval-count
  gap is just 1.4x; the wall gap (5.9x) is dominated by per-eval
  cost (~1.7ms vs ~0.13ms per eval). The per-eval-cost win belongs
  to interlace-7bxn (cache sparse patterns), not this issue.

- lme4 stage-2 Nelder-Mead defaults (R/optimizer.R:27-32) are
  *looser*, not tighter, than what interlace uses today:

    | Knob       | lme4 default | interlace today |
    |------------|--------------|-----------------|
    | maxfun     | 10000        | 2000            |
    | FtolAbs    | 1e-5         | 1e-7  (TIGHTER) |
    | FtolRel    | 1e-15        | (not set)       |
    | XtolRel    | 1e-7         | 1e-7            |
    | algorithm  | fixed N-M    | adaptive=True (Gao-Han) |

  interlace is over-converging the simplex on objective values
  by 100x relative to lme4. Fewer evals are needed once the
  tolerance is loosened to match lme4.

## What
Align Phase-2 Nelder-Mead with lme4 stage-2 conventions. Specific
changes:

1. Loosen fatol from 1e-7 to 1e-5 (= lme4 FtolAbs).
2. Add ftol_rel-equivalent if scipy supports it; otherwise rely on
   fatol and xatol.
3. Drop adaptive=True (lme4 uses a fixed Nelder-Mead; the adaptive
   variant adds evals at small n).
4. Leave maxiter=2000 in place. Real convergence happens around 250-400
   evals; the maxiter cap is defensive only and aligns with lme4 in
   spirit (both are "well above expected").
5. Sanity-check that nAGQ >= 2 already bypasses Phase 2 in interlace
   (in lme4, AGQ replaces the joint optimisation; verify the
   _agq_loglik path at glmm_laplace.py:1108 is reached without
   running Phase 2 too).

Do NOT add a "skip Phase 2 when easy" branch. lme4 does not, and
the test surface for "easy" is fragile (zero-inflated, obs-level RE,
binomial-with-many-categories all need Phase 2).

## Acceptance criteria
- Phase-2 eval count on CBPP within 1.5x of lme4 (lme4: 285;
  target: <= 430). Likely lands around 200-300 with looser fatol.
- CBPP fit time drops modestly (probably 10-25%); the bigger
  wall-time wins live with interlace-7bxn (sparse-pattern caching)
  and interlace-7sc3 (CHOLMOD on GLMM path).
- Validation suite still passes: FE abs diff <1e-3, VC rel <5%,
  BLUP corr >0.99, conditional residual corr >0.999.
- A new test asserts Phase-2 eval count for CBPP stays within
  some envelope (regression guard).
- Verify nAGQ >= 2 path bypasses Phase 2.

## Out of scope
- Skip-Phase-2 heuristics (rejected: diverges from lme4).
- Switching Phase 2 to bobyqa (lme4 supports it as an option but
  defaults to Nelder-Mead; revisit only if Phase 1+2 alignment
  is insufficient).
- Per-eval cost reduction -> belongs to interlace-7bxn / 7sc3.

## Reference
- lme4 source: R/optimizer.R:27 (Nelder_Mead defaults),
  R/lmer.R:154-198 (two-stage flow), R/modular.R:911-944
  (optimizeGlmer dispatcher), src/optimizer.cpp:291 (C++
  termination defaults; note: maxeval=300 default is
  *overridden* to 10000 by the R wrapper).
- Empirical lme4 CBPP measurement: 285 stage-2 evals, single fit.
- docs/perf/profiles/notes.md "New findings -> A".
close_reason: Aligned Phase-2 Nelder-Mead options with lme4 stage-2 defaults (commit f11e8a9). CBPP Phase-2 evals 405->208 (-49%), under lme4's 285. All 1446 tests pass; numerical agreement with lme4 preserved.

title: Profile Sleepstudy and CBPP fits to confirm hot spots
description:
## Why
Before committing to the optimizations under epic interlace-81ru, confirm
the hypothesised hot spots with real profile data. The 7x and 11x ratios
are concrete enough that one profile pass tells us whether the bottleneck
is spsolve, sparse construction, optimizer overhead, or PIRLS Python-loop
overhead -- and rank-orders the fixes.

## What
Run py-spy (and/or cProfile + snakeviz) on:
  - Sleepstudy random-slopes LMM fit (paper/replication.py path).
  - CBPP binomial GLMM fit (paper/replication.py path).

Capture for each:
  - Top-15 functions by cumulative time.
  - Top-15 by self time.
  - How many objective calls L-BFGS-B makes; how many PIRLS iterations
    inside each Laplace objective call on CBPP.
  - Whether sksparse.cholmod is actually being used (vs SuperLU fallback).

## Output
Save profile artefacts (svg flamegraphs + .prof files) under
`benchmarks/profiles/` in the manuscript repo (or under
`docs/perf/profiles/` here -- pick one). Write a short notes.md that
ranks the hypotheses in the epic body by confirmed % of wall time, so
follow-on tasks can be scoped accurately.

## Acceptance criteria
  - Flamegraphs committed for both Sleepstudy and CBPP fits.
  - Each Tier-1 hypothesis in epic interlace-81ru is annotated with
    "confirmed / partial / refuted" + observed share of wall time.
  - Iter counts (outer optimizer + inner PIRLS) reported.

## Notes
This task blocks the optimization tasks under the epic; everything
downstream is hypothesis-driven until this lands.
notes: Profile artefacts under docs/perf/profiles/. Top findings: (1) sparse-pattern rebuild = ~35-40% Sleepstudy / ~50-60% CBPP self-time (Tier-1 #7bxn = top win for both); (2) CBPP runs Phase-2 Nelder-Mead at 93% of wall time -- new candidate child issue, not currently in epic; (3) reml_gradient only implemented for diagonal Lambda, so jjm7 ('default analytic gradient on') needs the gradient generalised first or switch random-slopes to BOBYQA; (4) CHOLMOD does not affect glmm_laplace path (uses spla.spsolve directly), so 98ip and w1sl need to also touch glmm_laplace.py to help CBPP; (5) spsolve column-loop is only ~3% of CBPP wall (smaller win than expected). Re-ranked Tier-1 ordering in docs/perf/profiles/notes.md.
close_reason: Profile artefacts and notes committed at docs/perf/profiles/ -- all acceptance criteria met (flamegraphs, hypothesis verdicts, iter counts).

title: Batch multi-RHS sparse solves in PIRLS and gradient
description:
## Why
Likely largest single Tier-1 win for CBPP, and helps Sleepstudy too.
glmm_laplace.py rebuilds the LU/Cholesky factor of A every column:

  glmm_laplace.py:895
      np.column_stack([spla.spsolve(A, ZstWX[:, j]) for j in range(p)])
  glmm_laplace.py:897
      A_inv_ZstWz = spla.spsolve(A, ZstWz)
  glmm_laplace.py:1668
      np.column_stack([spla.spsolve(A, ZstWX[:, j]) for j in range(p)])

Each `spla.spsolve` redoes the symbolic+numeric factorisation. Inside
PIRLS (up to 100 iters) inside the outer theta optimizer, this is
multiplicative.

## What
Replace per-column spsolve loops with a single factorisation + multi-RHS
solve:

  - When sksparse.cholmod is available:
        factor.cholesky(A); X = factor(ZstWX); v = factor(ZstWz)
    (CHOLMOD natively accepts dense or sparse RHS matrices.)
  - Fallback: `lu = spla.splu(A); X = lu.solve(ZstWX_dense); v = lu.solve(ZstWz)`.

Audit profiled_reml.py for the same antipattern (e.g. _sparse_solve at
line ~246 used both for c1 and C_X separately -- consider a single
multi-RHS call against `np.column_stack([lZty[:, None], lZtX])`).

## Acceptance criteria
  - No remaining `[spsolve(A, M[:, j]) for j in range(p)]` patterns
    under src/interlace/.
  - All existing tests still pass (numerical equivalence preserved).
  - Sleepstudy and CBPP benchmarks rerun: per-iteration time drops.

## Risks / pitfalls
  - splu vs CHOLMOD codepath divergence: keep both, gated by import.
  - For very small p (e.g. p=1), the loop overhead is tiny; gain is
    concentrated where p > a few.
close_reason: Superseded by interlace-7sc3: CHOLMOD multi-RHS solves already implemented in _pirls (commit 1ee165e) and in profiled REML via chol_factor.solve(lZtX). Remaining SuperLU-fallback per-column loops are ~3-5% of wall time and on a non-production path; better addressed by interlace-98ip (require CHOLMOD).

comments.author: heliopais
comments.text: Assessment after 7sc3 (2026-05-07): PARTIALLY DONE -- the CHOLMOD path now does multi-RHS in one factor.solve(ZstWX) call (commit 1ee165e in _pirls). The SuperLU fallback path still has the per-column spsolve loop at glmm_laplace.py:900-902, but this code is rarely hit now that sksparse is near-required for production performance. Profile data showed the column-loop was only ~3-5% of CBPP wall even in the SuperLU baseline. Recommend close as superseded for the CHOLMOD path; keep open as P3 (was P1) only if/until SuperLU fallback becomes a measurable concern.

title: Performance: close the 7-11x gap vs lme4 on Sleepstudy/CBPP
description:
## Why
Section 4.3 (Performance benchmarks) in the JSS manuscript reports interlace
is 7.0x slower than lme4 on Sleepstudy (random-slopes LMM, n=180) and 10.8x
slower on CBPP (binomial GLMM, n=56). Random-intercept LMMs are at parity
(Dyestuff 1.3x, Radon 1.1x). The gap is concentrated in two paths:

  - profiled_reml.py: the random-slopes objective (sparse Cholesky / spsolve
    inner loop, called ~hundreds of times by L-BFGS-B).
  - glmm_laplace.py: the PIRLS inner loop inside the Laplace objective,
    which itself is called by the outer theta optimizer.

Closing this gap to ~2-3x preserves interlace's "pure-Python, scipy-only"
positioning while making it a credible drop-in for lme4 on realistic
problem sizes. Beyond ~3x is unlikely without giving up the pure-Python
story (lme4 is compiled C++/Eigen).

## Scope
Concrete suspected hot spots (from a static read; profile-confirm in the
first child task):

  - glmm_laplace.py:895,1668 -- `[spla.spsolve(A, M[:, j]) for j in range(p)]`
    refactorises A on every column. Multi-RHS solve is a single factor.
  - profiled_reml.py:226 (`sparse_chol_logdet`) -- uses scipy SuperLU even
    when A is SPD. CHOLMOD is plumbed in but only optional; the fallback
    is materially slower.
  - L-BFGS-B may be running without analytic gradient even though
    `reml_gradient` exists -- adds n_theta+1 extra objective evals per step.
  - Lambda / A11 / Z'WZ are rebuilt as fresh CSC matrices every objective
    call. Pattern is fixed across theta; only values change.
  - Sparse machinery overhead may dominate when q is small (CBPP: q=15).

## Approach (tiers; profile then attack in order)
  Tier 0: Profile (py-spy / cProfile) Sleepstudy and CBPP fits to
          confirm/falsify the hypotheses above before coding.
  Tier 1: Pure-Python wins -- batch multi-RHS solves, default analytic
          gradient, reuse CHOLMOD symbolic factor, cache sparse patterns.
  Tier 2: Make sksparse/CHOLMOD a hard dep (or [fast] extra) for the
          hard paths.
  Tier 3: Small-q dense fast path for A11 + LAPACK Cholesky.
  Tier 4 (last resort): Numba-jit the PIRLS inner kernel. Costs the
          pure-Python story; only if Tier 1-3 don't reach ~2-3x.

## Acceptance criteria
  - Sleepstudy ratio drops from 7.0x to <= 3x (target: <= 2x).
  - CBPP ratio drops from 10.8x to <= 3x (target: <= 2x).
  - Dyestuff and Radon stay within run-to-run noise of current numbers.
  - Numerical agreement with lme4 in benchmarks/results.tex unchanged
    (LMM FE abs diff < 1e-4, GLMM FE abs diff < 1e-3, VC rel < 5%,
     BLUP corr > 0.99).
  - Manuscript Section 4.3 prose + benchmarks/results.tex regenerated
    and committed in interlace-manuscript.

## Reference
Manuscript benchmark table (current):
  Dyestuff   n=30   0.008s vs 0.006s  (1.3x)
  Sleepstudy n=180  0.063s vs 0.009s  (7.0x)
  Radon      n=919  0.010s vs 0.009s  (1.1x)
  CBPP       n=56   0.414s vs 0.038s  (10.8x)

comments.author: heliopais
comments.text: Status after 7sc3 (2026-05-07): CBPP is at 1.6x lme4 on this host (0.180s vs 0.115s) -- past the 2x stretch target. Cumulative wall reduction from baseline: -74%. Sleepstudy is at noise floor on this host (~80-100ms) and needs re-measurement on a thermally stable machine before declaring its acceptance criterion met. Closed children: 1yyz (profile), 7bxn (Lambda+inner-loop pattern caching), w7b8 (Phase-2 lme4-aligned tolerances), 7sc3 (CHOLMOD on GLMM path). Remaining open: see comments on each. The technical work is essentially done; what's left is benchmarking discipline (buax) and a few low-priority polish items.

title: Satterthwaite degrees of freedom for fixed effects
description:
Implement Satterthwaite (and optionally Kenward-Roger) denominator degrees of freedom for fixed-effect t-tests and F-tests.

## Why

interlace currently computes fixed-effect p-values using a normal approximation (z-test), which is what lme4 itself does. However, the standard R workflow uses lmerTest on top of lme4, which provides Satterthwaite-approximated DFs — giving t-statistics and p-values that account for small-sample and unbalanced designs. Users migrating from R expect p-values that match lmerTest output, not raw z-tests.

## What needs to be done

- Implement Satterthwaite DF approximation: for each fixed-effect contrast c, compute
    DF_Satt = 2 * (c'Vc)^2 / Var(c'Vc)
  where the denominator requires the gradient of the variance of c'β̂ with respect to the covariance parameters θ (numerical differentiation of the REML Hessian is acceptable for v1).
- Add fe_df (Series of DFs per FE coef), fe_tvalues (FE coef / FE SE), fe_pvalues updated to use t-distribution with Satterthwaite DFs.
- Expose as summary() method that prints a formatted table matching lmerTest output.
- Kenward-Roger (bias-corrected VCV) is a stretch goal; Satterthwaite is the priority.

## Acceptance criteria

- fe_pvalues match lmerTest Satterthwaite p-values to <0.001 on sleepstudy and cbpp fixtures.
- Degrees of freedom are finite and positive for all fixed effects.
- summary() prints a readable table with Estimate, Std.Error, df, t value, Pr(>|t|).
close_reason: Implemented Satterthwaite DF approximation: fe_df attribute, t-distribution p-values, and updated summary() output with df/t value columns

title: ML objective + anova() model comparison
description:
Add maximum-likelihood (ML) fitting and a model-comparison API to interlace.

## Why

lme4 supports REML=FALSE to fit via ML, which is required for likelihood-ratio tests (LRT) between nested models. Currently interlace only implements the REML objective. Without ML fitting, users cannot do formal model comparison — a core part of mixed-model workflows in R.

## What needs to be done

- Implement ML profiled objective (vs current REML): the difference is that ML integrates over fixed effects rather than profiling them out, so log|X'V⁻¹X| term is dropped in REML but not ML.
- Expose via fit(..., method='ML') (method param already exists on the API; verify REML vs ML branching).
- Add anova(m1, m2) function that: validates m1 and m2 differ only in fixed effects (REML→ML refit required) or in random effects (REML ok), computes LRT statistic = 2*(llf2 - llf1), df = difference in param count, chi-sq p-value.
- Handle the lme4 warning: REML models must be refit with ML before LRT.

## Acceptance criteria

- fit(..., method='ML') converges and matches lme4 ML log-likelihood to <0.01.
- anova(m1, m2) returns a DataFrame/table with columns: Df, AIC, BIC, logLik, deviance, Chisq, Chi Df, Pr(>Chisq).
- Raises ValueError or warning when comparing REML-fitted models without refitting.
close_reason: ML fitting and anova() implemented, 25 tests passing

title: Fix leverage fixef for crossed RE: use OLS hat instead of block-diagonal GLS
description:
## Why

interlace.leverage(model)['fixef'] returns inflated values for CrossedLMEResult. The hat matrix trace is ~1.6x too large (e.g. 9.74 instead of 6 for p=6), causing downstream consumers to flag too many observations as high-leverage.

## Root cause

_crossed_structures groups observations by primary factor and computes Vi = ZiDZi' + sigma2*I per group. For crossed RE, V is NOT block-diagonal by primary group — observations in different primary groups can share another grouping factor. So sum_g Xi'Vi^-1 Xi \!= X'V^-1 X and trace(H1) \!= p.

## What needs to be done

For CrossedLMEResult, return the OLS hat matrix X(X'X)^-1 X' as fixef (consistent with R's HLMdiag which explicitly does not compute GLS leverage for crossed RE). The OLS hat has trace = p by construction.

## Acceptance criteria

- trace(h_fixef) == p (within 1e-10) for a crossed RE model
- Per-observation values match OLS hat diagonal exactly
- ranef and ranef.uc return zeros (conservative, consistent with HLMdiag)
- overall == fixef + ranef still holds
close_reason: Fixed: truly crossed RE (≥2 groups) now returns OLS hat for fixef; trace(H1)=p by construction. Single-group CrossedLMEResult keeps GLS path.

title: Joint Student-t × dispformula path: random_effects loses string labels, predict() ignores groupings
description:
## Summary
Two related issues in the joint Student-t × dispformula fit path (`student_t_dispformula_joint_laplace`, hit when calling `fit(family=\"student_t\", dispformula=...)` with random effects in either side).

### Bug 1: RE index loses string labels
On a plain LMM (no Student-t, no dispformula), `result.random_effects[<group>]` is a `pd.Series` indexed by the actual group labels — e.g. `'m00'`, `'m00:m00_s0'`, `'m00:m00_s0:m00_s0_t0'` for an `(1|main/sub/typ)` spec. Downstream code can look up the random intercept for a specific group with `series.loc[label]`.

On the joint Student-t × dispformula path, the same `random_effects` dict has integer-indexed Series (`Int64Index([0, 1, 2, ...])`). The level→integer mapping isn't exposed anywhere I could find on the result object. `result.lmm.random_effects` (the inner LMM at convergence) has the same integer index — so it's not just a wrapper-level issue.

This blocks any downstream code that needs to compute predictions for new data with the same hierarchical fallback semantics R's `predict.merMod(..., re.form=...)` provides.

### Bug 2: predict() on new data ignores grouping columns
`result.predict(newdata)` runs without error but appears to return only the **fixed-effect** contribution. Symptoms on a `(1|main/sub/typ)` model:
- A grid of rows with **distinct** `kldb_type` values but identical fixed-effect covariates returns *identical* predictions (one value, not one per `kldb_type`).
- `predict(df_train)` does not equal `result.fittedvalues` (they differ by a non-constant amount on training data).
- `predict()` on rows with **unseen** group levels also returns the same value as the seen-level rows, so it's clearly not doing nested fallback either.

### Reproducer
```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, interlace
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
rows = []
for mi in range(4):
    m = f\"m{mi:02d}\"
    main_re = rng.normal(0, 0.3)
    for si in range(3):
        s = f\"{m}_s{si}\"
        sub_re = main_re + rng.normal(0, 0.2)
        for ti in range(3):
            t = f\"{s}_t{ti}\"
            typ_re = sub_re + rng.normal(0, 0.15)
            for _ in range(15):
                rl = float(rng.integers(1, 5))
                y = 0.05 + 0.1*(rl-2.5) + typ_re + rng.standard_t(4.0)*0.15
                rows.append({\"main\": m, \"sub\": s, \"typ\": t, \"rl\": rl, \"rl_cat\": str(int(rl)), \"y\": y})
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
df[\"rl_std\"] = (df[\"rl\"] - df[\"rl\"].mean()) / df[\"rl\"].std()

res = interlace.fit(
    formula=\"y ~ rl_std\",
    random=[\"(1|main/sub/typ)\"],
    dispformula=\"~ (1|rl_cat)\",
    data=df,
    family=\"student_t\",
    method=\"REML\",
)
print(res.random_effects[\"main\"].index)     # Int64Index([0,1,2,3]) — expected: ['m00',...]
df_new = df.drop_duplicates(\"typ\")[:5].assign(rl_std=0.0)
print(res.predict(df_new))                    # five identical values
```

### Expected behaviour
- `result.random_effects[<group_key>]` should be indexed by the group label(s) (colon-joined for nested), matching the plain-LMM contract.
- `result.predict(newdata)` should include the relevant random-intercept contributions for each row's group memberships, with hierarchical fallback to coarser levels for unseen leaves.

### Workaround currently in use
Subtract `Intercept + Σ β_k x_ik` from `fittedvalues` to recover the *combined* RE per training row, then aggregate to type/sub/main levels and apply manual fallback. Works in-sample but is fiddly and depends on the user knowing this is necessary.

### Impact
Blocks straightforward replacement of an existing R `glmmTMB(family=t_family, dispformula=...)` / Stan model in a downstream pipeline that needs to apply the fit to all kldb codes (most of which appear in training, some don't). The plain-LMM, plain-dispformula, and plain-Student-t paths look fine; only the *composition* of Student-t with dispformula seems to lose label fidelity in the result object and break `predict()`.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Repro above yields string-labeled `random_effects` Series indices
- [ ] `res.predict(df)` agrees with `res.fittedvalues` to floating-point tolerance
- [ ] `res.predict(newdata)` on a grid with distinct group leaves and identical covariates returns distinct values (one per leaf), and the difference between them equals the corresponding random intercepts
- [ ] Unseen leaves at any nesting level fall back to the deepest available parent level (or fixed-only if none match)
- [ ] Tests added to `tests/test_student_t_dispformula_joint.py` covering all four points

### Related
- `interlace-hpzy` — closed feature that introduced this path
- `interlace-1t0v` — closed feature for joint Laplace
close_reason: Fixed. Three changes: (1) dispformula_joint._split_blups now indexes per-spec Series/DataFrames by sorted unique group labels (matching plain LMM result contract). (2) Both dispformula joint/BCA result builders now set _secondary_group_cols. (3) predict() walks _random_specs and uses group_array to derive interaction columns (e.g. 'main:sub') on the fly — fixing a latent pre-existing bug in plain LMM nested predict too. 6 new tests in test_student_t_dispformula_joint_re.py; 1585 tests total pass.

title: Compose Student-t family with dispformula in single fit()
description:
## Motivation
`v0.3.0` shipped both `family=\"student_t\"` and `dispformula=...` as standalone features in `interlace.fit()`. They are currently **mutually exclusive**: passing both, or trying to enable a dispersion model under a Student-t likelihood, isn't supported because the dispatcher in `__init__.py` routes them down separate branches and `student_t_fit()` has no `dispformula` argument.

For the salary-models scaling use case (and the broader robust-heteroscedastic mixed-model space), the joint behaviour is the load-bearing one — the dispersion model is what captures group-level differences in noise scale, and the Student-t tail is what makes the fit robust to outliers. Without composition, users have to pick robustness OR heteroscedasticity.

## Reference model
The Stan model this aims to displace (from the Stepstone salary-models scaling pipeline):

```r
glmmTMB(
  diff ~ 1 + reqlevel + management_grp + supervisor_grp,
  family      = t_family,
  dispformula = ~ (1 | reqlevel/kldb_main_group_req/kldb_group_req),
  data        = df1,
  weights     = ipf_weights
)
```

i.e. nested random intercepts on the *mean* side, **a different** nested random-intercept structure on the *log-σ* side, Student-t residuals with estimable `nu`, and observation weights throughout. `glmmTMB` supports this jointly; interlace currently does not.

## API sketch
Minimal change — relax the current branching in `fit()` so `family=\"student_t\"` can be combined with `dispformula`:

```python
result = fit(
    formula     = \"diff ~ reqlevel + management_grp + supervisor_grp\",
    dispformula = \"~ (1 | g1/g2/g3)\",
    data        = df,
    groups      = [\"main\", \"group\", \"type\"],
    family      = \"student_t\",
    weights     = df[\"ipf_weights\"].values,
)

print(result.nu)
print(result.fe_params)
print(result.disp_fe_params)
print(result.disp_variance_components)
```

## Implementation notes
Three plausible routes, in increasing order of effort:

1. **EM with per-observation latent scale + heteroscedastic LMM E-step.**
   The latent-scale formulation of the t-distribution gives
   `tau_i ~ Gamma(nu/2, nu/2)`, `y_i | tau_i, sigma_i ~ N(mu_i, sigma_i^2 / tau_i)`.
   In the E-step, `tau_i` has a closed-form conditional posterior (Gamma).
   In the M-step the mean update is a weighted Gaussian LMM with effective weights
   `w_i_eff = base_w_i * E[tau_i] / sigma_i^2` — which is exactly the existing
   `dispformula_bca.py` mean update if we pass the t-adjusted weights in.
   The dispformula step (fit gamma-GLMM on squared residuals) needs a small change to
   account for `E[tau_i]` in its sufficient statistics. `nu` is updated by the same
   1-D Brent search already in `student_t.py`.
   This reuses the existing BCA scaffolding and is probably the lowest-risk shape.

2. **Joint Laplace generalisation.**
   Extend `dispformula_joint.py`'s joint latent `(b, d)` Hessian to a t-likelihood:
   the per-observation contribution `student_t_lpdf(y | nu, mu_i, sigma_i)` plugs in
   with analytic gradients. More accurate inference (SEs, profile CIs); more work.

3. **Reuse `glmm_laplace.py` by adding a `StudentTFamily` with a per-obs `sigma_i`
   passed via offset/working-response machinery.**
   Cleanest in principle but probably requires the most plumbing.

Suggested first cut: route 1 under `dispformula_method=\"bca\"`, then route 2 under
the default `\"joint_laplace\"` for proper marginalisation.

## Parity target
Validate vs `glmmTMB(..., family = t_family, dispformula = ...)` on 2-3 fixtures
including the salary use case:
- abs diff < 1e-3 on mean-model fixed effects and `nu`
- rel diff < 5% on mean-side variance components
- rel diff < 10% on dispformula variance components (consistent with the standalone
  dispformula tolerances)

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `fit(..., family=\"student_t\", dispformula=\"~ ...\")` no longer raises and produces a fitted result
- [ ] Both `family=\"student_t\"` paths (`nu` estimated and `nu` fixed) compose with both `dispformula_method`s (`joint_laplace` and `bca`)
- [ ] Observation weights remain supported through the composed path
- [ ] Result object exposes `nu`, `fe_params`, `disp_fe_params`, `variance_components`, `disp_variance_components`
- [ ] Validation tests against R `glmmTMB` reference fits within the tolerances above
- [ ] Documentation: a section in the changelog and a short quickstart snippet — ideally a worked example mirroring the salary-models scaling formula (with synthetic data)

## Related

- `interlace-znql` — dispformula support (closed)

title: Add dispformula support: model log(sigma) with fixed+random effects
description:
## Motivation
Add support for a second formula that models the (log) residual scale, mirroring R's `glmmTMB(..., dispformula = ~ <predictors> + (1|g1/g2))`. This lets users fit heteroscedastic mixed models where the noise variance itself depends on covariates and/or grouping factors.

Currently interlace supports AR(1) and compound-symmetry residual correlation structures (per README), but not a covariate-driven dispersion model with its own random effects.

## Real-world driver
A salary-modelling pipeline (Stepstone `salary-models`, scaling pipeline) fits a Stan model:
```r
m6 <- glmmTMB(diff ~ 1 + reqlevel + management_grp + supervisor_grp,
              data = df1,
              family = t_family,                     # see sibling issue
              dispformula = ~ (1|reqlevel/kldb_main_group_req/kldb_group_req),
              weights = ipf_weights)
```
The dispersion side captures the empirically observed pattern that residual variance differs systematically across requirement levels and occupational groups. Without `dispformula`, downstream scale-factor estimates degrade because uniform `sigma` over-shrinks high-variance cells and under-shrinks low-variance ones.

## API sketch
```python
result = fit(
    formula="y ~ x1 + x2",
    dispformula="~ x1 + (1|g1/g2)",   # new
    data=df,
    groups=["g0"],
)

print(result.fe_params)                 # mean-model coefficients
print(result.disp_fe_params)            # dispersion-model coefficients (on log scale)
print(result.disp_variance_components)  # dispersion-side variance components
```

Minimum useful subset for the salary use case:
- intercept + random intercepts only on the dispersion side (no fixed-effect predictors required)
- nested grouping shorthand (`a/b`) on the dispersion side
- coexists with observation weights

## Implementation notes
- Internally, `log_sigma_i = w_i'γ + v_i'd` with `d ~ N(0, H)`.
- For Gaussian-conditional models, the conditional log-likelihood is
  `-0.5 * [ log(2π) + 2 log_sigma_i + ((y_i - mu_i)^2 / exp(2 log_sigma_i)) ]`
  with weights as a multiplicative prefactor.
- Joint estimation is no longer a separable LMM. Options:
  1. Block-coordinate ascent: alternate mean-model (weighted LMM with current `sigma_i`) and dispersion-model (gamma-GLMM on squared residuals). Easy to layer on existing machinery; converges robustly when initialised from homoscedastic fit.
  2. Joint Laplace: extend `glmm_laplace.py` to a two-block latent state `(b, d)` with a joint Hessian. More work but more accurate inference (SEs, profile CIs).
- Pairs naturally with the Student-t family issue: in that case `sigma_i` is the t-distribution scale.

## Reference implementation
- R `glmmTMB` `dispformula` argument — most natural target for parity.

## Parity target
- abs diff < 1e-3 on mean-model fixed effects
- rel diff < 10% on dispersion variance components (these are notoriously harder to identify)
- Validate against `glmmTMB(..., dispformula = ~ (1|g))` on 1-2 small datasets

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `fit()` accepts a `dispformula` argument (`str` parsed with the same nested-group shorthand as the mean formula)
- [ ] Result object exposes `disp_fe_params` and `disp_variance_components` (or equivalent)

- [ ] Works in combination with the Student-t family (sibling issue) — `sigma_i` becomes the t scale parameter
- [ ] Validation tests vs R `glmmTMB(..., dispformula = ...)` within tolerances above
- [ ] Documentation page (concept + quickstart snippet)

## Out of scope (follow-ups)
- Dispersion-side random slopes
- Profile CIs on dispersion variance components (can ship later)

title: Add Student-t (robust) family for LMM/GLMM
description:
## Motivation
Add a Student-t response family with estimable degrees-of-freedom (`nu`) for robust mixed-effects regression. This matches R's `glmmTMB(..., family = t_family)` and is the canonical way to handle heavy-tailed residuals or outliers without manual winsorisation.

## Real-world driver
A downstream salary-modelling pipeline (Stepstone `salary-models`, scaling pipeline) currently uses cmdstanpy with a Stan model that combines:
  - nested random intercepts `(1|kldb_main/kldb_group/kldb_type)` — interlace already supports this
  - a Student-t likelihood with estimable `nu` (~2-10 typically) for robustness against compensation outliers
  - observation weights (IPF weights for sample bias correction) — interlace already supports

Replacing Stan with interlace would eliminate the CmdStan toolchain dependency, but only if a t-family is available. The pipeline fits via L-BFGS optimisation (point estimates), so MCMC is not required — a frequentist robust LMM via REML/ML maximum-likelihood is sufficient.

## API sketch
```python
result = fit(
    formula="diff ~ reqlevel + management_grp + supervisor_grp",
    data=df,
    groups=["kldb_main/kldb_group/kldb_type"],
    family="student_t",       # new
    weights=df["ipf_weights"].values,
    df_method="satterthwaite",
)
print(result.nu)              # estimated degrees of freedom
```
Or via an explicit family object: `family=StudentTFamily(nu=None)` with `nu=None` → estimate, otherwise fixed.

## Implementation notes
- The conditional likelihood is `student_t(y | nu, mu_i, sigma)`; for an LMM-style model `mu_i = x_i'β + z_i'b` and `b ~ N(0, G)`.
- Marginal likelihood is no longer closed-form (no Gaussian conjugacy), so REML loses its tractable profile. Two viable routes:
  1. Treat as GLMM with identity link → Laplace approximation / adaptive Gauss-Hermite (interlace already has `glmm_laplace.py`). Add `StudentTFamily` to `glmm_family.py` with appropriate variance / deviance functions and unit-scale parameter.
  2. EM with latent scale per observation (`tau_i ~ Gamma(nu/2, nu/2)`, `y_i | tau_i ~ N(x_i'β + z_i'b, sigma^2/tau_i)`) → reduces to weighted LMM at each E-step, reusing existing REML machinery.
- Both routes need to also estimate `nu`. Route 2 fits naturally because the E-step gives a closed-form update for the latent precisions and `nu` can be optimised via a 1-D root-find on the profiled likelihood.

## Reference implementations
- R `glmmTMB::t_family` (TMB-based marginal likelihood)
- R `heavy::heavyLme` (EM-based, the latent-scale formulation)
- Lange, K. L., Little, R. J., & Taylor, J. M. (1989). Robust statistical modeling using the t distribution. JASA.

## Parity target
Validate against `glmmTMB(..., family = t_family)` on a couple of small benchmarks:
- abs diff < 1e-3 on fixed effects
- rel diff < 5% on variance components and `nu`

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `StudentTFamily` class added to `glmm_family.py` (or a route-2 wrapper around `fit()`)
- [ ] `fit()` / `glmer()` accept `family="student_t"`
- [ ] `nu` is either estimable or settable as a fixed positive scalar (>2)
- [ ] Observation weights supported (multiplicative on log-likelihood contributions)
- [ ] Result object exposes `nu` (or equivalent) and standard fixed/variance outputs
- [ ] Validation tests against an R reference fit on 1-2 datasets, within tolerances above
- [ ] Documentation page or quickstart section
notes: Implemented Student-t LMM via EM with latent scales (route 2). Each EM iteration is a weighted Gaussian LMM (M-step) + closed-form posterior tau (E-step); nu estimated via interleaved 1-D Brent on profile log-lik (ECM). Exposed as student_t_fit() and via fit(..., family='student_t'). 8 tests pass; full suite 1558 pass; lint+typecheck clean.

title: Numba-JIT'd selected inverse on pattern(ZtZ) for reml_gradient (Phase B of mxzk)
description:
## Why
Phase A of interlace-mxzk reused the cached CHOLMOD factor in reml_gradient and removed two redundant SuperLU factorisations, making one gradient call ~2x faster. End-to-end `fit_reml` with `use_gradient=True` is still a regression vs forward-difference at q >= ~35 (q=180 ~0.85x, q=300 ~0.66x) because L-BFGS-B's FD path is fast when the objective is cheap. As a result, `use_gradient=None` currently resolves to `False` -- analytic is correct but not the default.

## What
Replace the dense `A11_inv = factor.solve(eye(q), 'A')` call in `reml_gradient` with a selected inverse computed via the Erisman-Tinney / Takahashi recursion on the sparsity pattern of `ZtZ`. Pure-Python prototype (`docs/perf/probes/test_selected_inverse.py`) is correct (max abs diff 8e-17 vs np.linalg.inv on pattern) but ~8x slower than `solve(eye, 'A')` at q=180 due to Python loop overhead -- so this needs to be JIT-compiled. Numba is the lightest path (single function, lower-level than Cython).

## Acceptance criteria
- Numba added as an optional `[fast]` extra (or required dep, TBD).
- `reml_gradient` selected-inverse path produces values matching `np.linalg.inv` to <= 1e-10 on `pattern(ZtZ)`.
- End-to-end `fit_reml(use_gradient=True)` is faster than `use_gradient=False` at q in {80, 180, 300} on `docs/perf/probes/bench_gradient_inverse.py`.
- Flip the auto-detect default in `fit_reml`: `use_gradient=None` resolves to `is_diagonal` (i.e. on for intercept-only specs).
- All existing gradient tests still pass (`check_grad` rtol < 1e-3).

## Notes
- Takahashi recursion: for `A = P^T L L^T P`, compute `Z[i,j] = (A^{-1})[i,j]` for `(i,j) in pattern(L+L^T)` by descending column j and using already-computed Z[k,i] entries with k>j. Pseudocode and pure-Python reference impl in `docs/perf/probes/test_selected_inverse.py`.
- `pattern(ZtZ) is subset pattern(L+L^T)` after CHOLMOD's fill-reducing permutation, so all needed lookups are reachable.
- Spawned from interlace-mxzk Phase A close-out.

title: Optimize reml_gradient: avoid dense O(q^3) A11_inv
description:
## Why
Per benchmark probe under interlace-jjm7 (2026-05-08), the analytic REML gradient is correct but slower than forward-difference at q>=80 because reml_gradient computes `A11_inv = lu.solve(np.eye(q))` once per gradient call (profiled_reml.py:598). At q=180 this dominates: speedup is 0.7x vs FD even though obj-call count drops 67%. This is why we cannot flip use_gradient=True as the default.

## What
Rewrite the trace computations in reml_gradient to avoid the dense q*q inverse. Two viable approaches:

1. **Selective inverse via CHOLMOD**: cholmod.cho_factor(A11) then extract only the entries of A11^{-1} on the sparsity pattern of dA11_k. Sufficient because tr(A11^{-1} dA11_k) = sum_{i,j in pattern} A11_inv[i,j] * dA11_k[i,j].

2. **Hutchinson-style stochastic trace estimator**: tr(A11^{-1} dA11_k) ~ E[v' A11^{-1} dA11_k v] using a few random Rademacher v vectors. May be sufficient since the gradient feeds into L-BFGS-B which is robust to noise.

## Acceptance criteria
- reml_gradient wall-time at q=180 is <= reml_objective wall-time (i.e. one gradient call no slower than one obj call).
- check_grad still passes existing tolerance (rtol < 1e-3 / 1e-4).
- After this lands, flip use_gradient default to True (auto-detect for slopes via the same plumbing) and re-run the benchmark probe to confirm wall-time speedup.

## Notes
The use_gradient=None auto-detect machinery was prototyped under jjm7 and reverted because the underlying gradient was not faster. When we revisit, the plumbing pattern (use_gradient: bool | None = None, resolve based on `is_diagonal = specs is None or all(s.n_terms == 1 for s in specs)`) is the right shape -- raise NotImplementedError if explicit True with slopes, auto-False for slopes if None.

title: Route GLMM (glmm_laplace.py) through CHOLMOD when available
description:
## Why
Profiling under interlace-1yyz revealed that all sparse solves in
glmm_laplace.py call spla.spsolve directly (lines 895, 897, 1066,
1668), bypassing the _try_cholmod() machinery that profiled_reml.py
uses for LMMs. As a result, sister tasks interlace-98ip (CHOLMOD as
hard dep) and interlace-w1sl (reuse symbolic factor) currently buy
0% on CBPP/GLMM workloads even after they land for LMM.

This is a correctness/architecture gap: the GLMM hot path does
not benefit from the optional CHOLMOD acceleration that the LMM
path does.

## What
- Plumb a CHOLMOD-aware solve helper into glmm_laplace.py so the
  spla.spsolve calls in PIRLS (line 1066) and the column-loop
  solves (lines 895, 1668) use sksparse.cholmod when available,
  falling back to spla.spsolve when not.
- Reuse symbolic factor across PIRLS iterations within one outer

- Once interlace-t3er (multi-RHS spsolve) lands, ensure the

title: Small-q dense fast path for A11 / Cholesky
description:
## Why
CBPP has q = 15 (15 herds, single random intercept). At that size, the
constant overhead of scipy.sparse machinery (CSC construction, indexing,
dispatch) dwarfs the actual factorisation work. A dense LAPACK Cholesky
on a 15x15 matrix is essentially free.

Heuristic: when q <= some threshold (try 200; tune), build A11 as a
dense ndarray and use scipy.linalg.cho_factor / cho_solve. Skip the
sparse codepath entirely.

## What
  - In profiled_reml._build_A11 / reml_objective: branch on q. For
    q <= threshold, materialise dense.
  - Same branch in glmm_laplace._laplace_objective_profiled and _pirls.
  - Tune threshold empirically against benchmark suite. Likely the
    crossover is somewhere between q=100 and q=500 depending on
    sparsity density.

## Acceptance criteria
  - CBPP benchmark drops materially (target: closes most of the
    remaining gap after Tier 1).
  - Dyestuff (q=6) and Radon (q=85) at parity or better with current.
  - Sleepstudy (q=36) at parity or better.
  - Larger fixtures (e.g. tests with q=1000+) unaffected or faster.

## Pitfalls
  - Lambda for correlated random slopes is block-diagonal sparse;
    "dense" really means dense A11, not dense Lambda. Keep Lambda as
    sparse but allow `(Lambda @ ZtZ @ Lambda).toarray()` early when q
    is small.
  - Memory: q^2 doubles dense; threshold of 1000 is 8 MB which is fine.

All 1475 tests pass; new test_glmm_dense_kernel.py asserts kernel parity and dispatcher routing. Step 2 (profiled_reml dense path for LMM small-q) remains open under this issue.

title: Cache Lambda / Z structural sparse patterns; mutate values only
description:
## Why
profiled_reml.make_lambda (line 82) builds a fresh sparse CSC every
objective call. The non-zero pattern of Lambda_theta is fully
determined by the random-effects spec and does not depend on theta;
only the values do. Same for the joint Z built by
sparse_z.build_joint_z_from_specs.

Constructing CSC from scratch (COO -> CSC conversion, sort, dedup)
each call is pure overhead inside a hot loop.

## What

    object holding (indptr, indices, value-write map). Per call,
    overwrite the .data array in place from a packed theta vector
    via the precomputed map.
  - Same treatment for any other sparse matrices built inside the
    objective.

## Acceptance criteria
  - make_lambda call cost (measured by cProfile cumulative time on
    a 100-iter Sleepstudy fit) drops by >5x.
  - Numerical outputs bitwise unchanged.

title: Promote sksparse/CHOLMOD to required dep for hard paths (or [fast] extra)
description:
## Why
sparse_chol_logdet (profiled_reml.py:226) currently uses scipy
SuperLU even for SPD matrices. CHOLMOD is materially faster for SPD
sparse Cholesky AND supports cheap symbolic/numeric separation
(see interlace-{cholmod-task}). Today CHOLMOD is optional; if the
benchmark machine lacks sksparse, users hit the slow path silently.

The "pure-Python, scipy-only" positioning is a feature, but on the
hard paths (random-slopes LMM, Laplace GLMM) the gap to lme4 is
unrecoverable without CHOLMOD.

## Options (pick one)
  A. Hard runtime dep: add sksparse to install_requires. Simplest, but
     sksparse wheels are awkward on some platforms (needs SuiteSparse).
  B. Optional extra: pip install interlace-lme[fast] adds sksparse.
     Loud (not silent) warning at fit() time on the hard paths if
     sksparse is missing -- e.g. "interlace will be ~5-10x slower
     without sksparse; install with: pip install interlace-lme[fast]".
  C. Vendor a tiny pure-Python LDL^T for SPD as a better fallback than
     SuperLU, keep sksparse optional. (More code to maintain.)

Recommend B unless wheel availability has improved.

## Acceptance criteria
  - pyproject.toml updated; CI exercises both paths.
  - Warning at fit() time when on the slow path for random-slopes
    or GLMM models (not just at import time -- users should see it
    during their first slow fit).
  - README + docs updated with one line on the [fast] extra.

## Notes
Scope decision tied to interlace's distribution story; flag for human
discussion before implementing.
close_reason: Shipped [fast] extra alias + one-shot fit-time warning on slow paths (random-slopes LMM, GLMM Laplace). README + CI updated. 1550 tests pass.

title: Reuse CHOLMOD symbolic factor across theta evaluations
description:
## Why
The sparsity pattern of A11 = I + W'W (and equivalently of the PIRLS
system Z'WZ + Lambda^{-1}) is fixed across theta -- only the values
change. CHOLMOD separates analyze (symbolic, expensive) from
factorize/refactor (numeric, cheap). Doing analyze once and refactor
per theta is the standard idiom and is what lme4 does.

profiled_reml.py:183 (_init_chol_factor) is called once per fit; need
to confirm we then refactor only (factor.cholesky(A11) for old API,
factor.factorize(A11) for new API) inside the inner loop without
re-analyzing.

## What
  - Audit fit_reml + reml_objective + reml_gradient: ensure the CHOLMOD
    factor object is created once (with the correct ordering /
    permutation) and only refactored numerically per theta.
  - Same audit for the PIRLS path in glmm_laplace.py: inside the inner
    loop A is rebuilt with new weights each iteration; the symbolic
    factor of A should be reused across PIRLS iterations and across
    outer theta evaluations.
  - Document the contract in module docstrings.

## Acceptance criteria
  - cProfile shows time spent in CHOLMOD analyze drops from
    O(outer_iters * pirls_iters) to O(1) per fit.
  - All numerical results unchanged.

## Pitfalls
  - If CHOLMOD's chosen permutation depends on numerical values
    (it shouldn't for AMD/COLAMD on the pattern, but verify), reusing
    can sometimes hurt. Test on Sleepstudy and a multi-term fixture.
close_reason: Already done in interlace-7sc3 commit 1ee165e. _CholmodHandle in glmm_laplace.py builds symbolic factor once via _make_cholmod_handle(A0) and calls refactor(A) (numeric-only via factor.factorize/cholesky) per inner eval. profiled_reml.py caches chol_factor and reuses it the same way. Verified by code inspection.

comments.author: heliopais
comments.text: Assessment after 7sc3 (2026-05-07): DONE -- subsumed by 7sc3 commit 1ee165e. The _CholmodHandle in glmm_laplace.py builds the symbolic factor once at fit start (from a representative A0 with theta=ones) and calls handle.refactor(A) per inner objective evaluation, which does numeric-only refactorisation reusing the symbolic ordering. The LMM path in profiled_reml.py already had this via _init_chol_factor at fit_reml setup. Recommend close as duplicate/done.

title: Default analytic gradient for L-BFGS-B; verify it is used
description:
## Why
profiled_reml.py defines `reml_gradient` (line 452). Need to verify it is
actually wired into `scipy.optimize.minimize(..., jac=...)` for the
default optimizer="lbfgsb" path. If not, L-BFGS-B falls back to forward
finite differences -- costing n_theta+1 extra objective evaluations
per gradient step. For a 3-parameter random-slopes Sleepstudy model
that is ~4x of inner work per outer step that is wasted.

## What
  - Trace fit_reml(...) -> verify `jac=reml_gradient` is passed when
    optimizer == "lbfgsb".
  - If not, plumb it in; gate behind `use_grad: bool = True` if a kill
    switch is wanted for debugging.
  - Add a test that monkey-patches reml_objective to count calls and
    asserts the lbfgsb path uses < (n_theta + 1) * step_count
    objective calls (i.e., gradient is providing derivatives, not FD).
  - Confirm gradient is correct via scipy.optimize.check_grad on a
    small fixture (already may exist in tests/).

## Acceptance criteria
  - lbfgsb path provably uses analytic gradient.
  - check_grad < 1e-5 on Sleepstudy fixture.
  - Sleepstudy benchmark improves measurably (target: 30%+ fewer
    objective calls).

## Notes
Cheap, low-risk Tier-1 win. Independent of the spsolve batching task.
close_reason: Wiring verified (jac is plumbed at profiled_reml.py:809-811). Default flip evaluated and reverted: benchmark probe across q=20..180, n=600..20000 showed analytic gradient reduces obj-call count 50-75% but wall time is flat-to-negative (0.7x at q=180) due to dense A11_inv = lu.solve(np.eye(q)) per gradient call (line 598). Spawned interlace-mxzk to optimize the gradient body before re-attempting the default flip. Side benefit: exposed and fixed a latent bug in _sparse_solve where spla.spsolve squeezes (q,1) RHS to (q,), breaking C_X @ beta_hat for intercept-only-X + crossed-RE configurations.

comments.author: heliopais
comments.text: Assessment after 7sc3 (2026-05-07): Re-scoped sharply. Originally 'turn analytic gradient on by default' to fix Sleepstudy's ~54% finite-difference cost. After 7bxn, Sleepstudy is at noise floor on this host (~80-100ms wall) so the relative gain has shrunk substantially. Two further blockers: (a) reml_gradient at profiled_reml.py:452 is ONLY implemented for the diagonal Lambda case; Sleepstudy is random-slopes, so the analytic gradient must be generalised first -- a non-trivial derivation. (b) CBPP is gradient-free entirely (Phase-2 = Nelder-Mead); zero impact there. Recommend downgrade to P3 or close. The cheap alternative -- switch the random-slopes path to BOBYQA (already supported in fit_reml) -- might capture most of the win without writing the gradient.

title: profile_confint reports CIs on theta (Cholesky-factor) scale instead of natural variance/SD scale
description:
profile_confint(m) returns the relative Cholesky-factor entries as the parameter estimates, e.g. for sleepstudy 'Reaction ~ Days + (1+Days|Subject)':

  Subject.L[(Intercept),(Intercept)]   0.9292   [0.5629, 1.4838]
  Subject.L[Days,(Intercept)]          0.0182   [0.0000, 0.1599]
  Subject.L[Days,Days]                 0.2226   [0.1450, 0.3449]

The docstring (profile_ci.py:153-156) acknowledges this: 'Parameters are reported on the theta (relative Cholesky factor) scale. For intercept-only specs, sigma_b ≈ theta * sqrt(sigma2_hat).' Users (and JSS reviewers) coming from lme4 expect confint(m) to report on the natural scale: '.sig01' / '.sig02' / '.sigma' as standard deviations, '.cor' as correlation. Cholesky-factor scale is opaque — the off-diagonal entry 0.0182 is not directly interpretable as a correlation.

This makes profile_confint hard to use as advertised. Profile-likelihood CIs in lme4 are the standard reference here.

Discovered while writing JSS manuscript code blocks for §5.5 (interlace-manuscript issue 530, B4).
acceptance_criteria: profile_confint returns CIs on the natural variance/SD/correlation scale by default (matching lme4's confint(m, method='profile')), with row labels users can read directly. If preserving theta-scale output is desired, support it via an opt-in parameter (e.g. scale='theta').
notes: Implementation sketch: after computing endpoint values for each theta_i, transform to natural scale by multiplying intercept thetas by sqrt(sigma2_hat) and converting correlation thetas via the Cholesky-to-correlation map. Variances are theta**2 * sigma2_hat for diagonal entries. Sigma also needs a row (residual SD).
close_reason: Fixed: natural scale output with correct sigma at boundary; namespace export added

title: Fit-result attributes (fe_params, VarCorr, …) always return pandas regardless of input backend
description:
The narwhals integration is documented as DataFrame-agnostic. The package docstrings (e.g. _frame.py:1-5: "return results in the same native type") and the JSS manuscript §3.7 (interlace-manuscript/interlace-body.tex:680-689) both claim that 'output DataFrames are returned in the same backend as the input'. Empirically this holds for row-aligned augmented frames (augment.py, residuals.py, leverage.py, influence.py — all use _frame.to_native(..., like=input)) but NOT for structural fit-result attributes, which are hardcoded pandas regardless of input.

Verified by feeding a polars frame through interlace.fit('y ~ x', df_pl, groups='g'):
  - result.fe_params              → pandas.Series  (always)
  - VarCorr(result).as_dataframe() → pandas.DataFrame (always)
  - fe_bse, fe_pvalues, fe_conf_int, random_effects → pandas (per result.py:81-95 docstring)

Numerical correctness is unaffected — values are identical for polars vs pandas input. The issue is purely behavioral/documentation: a polars-only project ends up with mixed-backend objects, and our docs (and the manuscript) overstate what's delivered.
acceptance_criteria: Either (a) make all DataFrame/Series outputs on MixedLMResults round-trip to the input backend (using _frame.native_from_dict / a polars-aware Series builder), so polars input yields polars outputs end-to-end; or (b) tighten the docstrings and JSS §3.7 prose to specify which outputs follow the input backend (augmented/diagnostic frames) versus which are always pandas (fit-result attributes).
notes: Discovered while writing a polars example for the JSS manuscript (interlace-manuscript issue n1z, B5). Picking option (a) is the more user-friendly fix but requires touching every fit-result attribute constructor; option (b) is a 1-2 sentence prose patch and unblocks the manuscript task immediately. The manuscript task is currently blocked on this decision.
close_reason: Option (b): updated _frame.py and result.py docstrings to clearly state fit-result attributes (fe_params, fe_bse, fe_pvalues, fe_df, fe_conf_int, random_effects) are always pandas regardless of input backend. Added regression test suite in tests/test_backend_compat.py contracting this behavior. Augmented/diagnostic frames continue to follow the input backend.

title: emmeans: at={col: [list]} silently broken for spec columns
description: Calling `interlace.emmeans(model, specs='X', at={'X': [v1, v2, v3]})` where X is a continuous predictor in specs crashes inside formulaic with 'unhashable type: list'. In _build_reference_grid (emmeans.py:184-192), level_lists enumerates ALL unique observed values for spec columns, then 'other_defaults.update(at)' adds the list as the value, then 'row.update(other_defaults)' overwrites the per-row spec value back to the list literal. The list is then passed to formulaic.model_matrix, which tries to make a categorical of a list and explodes. Either (a) raise a clear error when at[k] is a list and k is in specs, or (b) (preferred) override level_lists for that spec when at[k] is list-like. Discovered while writing JSS manuscript example for §5.2 CBPP / §5.3 sleepstudy — the natural call `emmeans(m, specs='Days', at={'Days': [0,4,9]})` is silently broken.
close_reason: Fixed: split at-dict handling in _build_reference_grid — list-like values for spec columns now replace level_lists[idx] instead of landing in other_defaults. 3 new tests added and passing.

title: Investigate Poisson OLRE parity gap (Ch 15 roaches model)
description:
The overdispersed Poisson GLMM with 262 observation-level random effects on the roaches dataset shows larger-than-expected differences vs R lme4::glmer(): FE diffs ~0.1-0.3, loglik gap ~2.9. This is the worst parity result across all Gelman & Hill validation models. Investigate root causes and improve convergence.

Possible avenues:
- Compare Laplace approximation implementation details (PIRLS inner loop convergence, step-halving)
- Try AGQ with nAGQ>1 (may not apply since 262 RE levels, but worth checking)
- Compare theta optimization trajectory (L-BFGS-B vs R's default optimizer)
- Check if the issue is in the sparse Cholesky with 262x262 Lambda vs R's approach
- Profile the objective function around R's optimum to see if interlace's objective differs
- Check whether the offset handling in the GLMM Laplace code introduces a discrepancy

Reference fixtures: tests/fixtures/gh_ch15_poisson_results.json (R theta=2.208, loglik=-896.40)
Current interlace result: theta~2.18, loglik=-899.28
notes:
## Extended Investigation (2026-04-21, continued)

### Additional findings
1. **R nAGQ=0 matches interlace exactly**: R's nAGQ=0 gives ll=-899.28, theta=2.177, beta=[1.358, 1.495, -0.694, -0.838] — identical to interlace.

2. **R nAGQ=1 uses two-phase optimization**: 
   - Phase 1 (nAGQ=0): bobyqa optimizer over theta only, PIRLS for (beta,u) jointly
   - Phase 2 (nAGQ=1): Nelder-Mead over (theta, beta) jointly (5 params!), with u from PIRLS inner loop
   The NM verbose output confirmed R optimizes 5 parameters in phase 2.

3. **Alternating PIRLS doesn't help**: the same local mode is found regardless of whether we solve (beta,v) jointly or alternately. The basin of attraction is universal for all PIRLS variants.

4. **Root cause is the joint (theta,beta) optimization in phase 2**: R's phase 2 moves beta directly via the outer optimizer (NM), not via PIRLS. This allows beta to escape the local mode that PIRLS gets stuck in.

### Fix
Implement lme4's two-phase approach in fit_glmm:
- Phase 1 (current): optimize theta with L-BFGS-B, PIRLS for (beta,u)  
- Phase 2: optimize (theta,beta) jointly via NM, with PIRLS for u only (given beta from outer loop)

This requires modifying the outer optimization in fit_glmm to include beta in the parameter vector for a second optimization pass.
close_reason: Fixed. Root cause: PIRLS multimodality with many obs-level REs. Added Phase 2 profiled optimization (_laplace_objective_profiled) that optimizes (theta, beta) jointly via Nelder-Mead with PIRLS solving u only. Roaches model gap: 2.9 → 0.001 loglik, FE diffs: 0.1-0.3 → 2e-4. All 1018 tests pass.

title: Analytical REML gradient for L-BFGS-B
description:
## Why this issue exists

L-BFGS-B currently uses finite differences to approximate the gradient of the profiled REML objective (reml_objective in profiled_reml.py). Each finite-difference gradient requires p+1 function evaluations (one per theta parameter plus the base), so a 4-theta model needs ~5 evals per L-BFGS-B step. This drives total eval counts to ~65-75 per refit (~17ms for the large_scale fixture).

Providing an analytical gradient via jac= reduces L-BFGS-B to ~1 eval per step (function + gradient together), cutting total evals to ~12-15 and halving per-refit time.

## What needs to be done

Derive and implement reml_gradient(theta, ...) — the analytical gradient of the profiled REML deviance with respect to theta.

The profiled REML deviance is:

  obj(theta) = log|A11| + log|MX| + (n-p) * log(y'Py)

where:
  A11 = Lambda' Z'Z Lambda + I_q
  MX  = X'X - (Lambda Z'X)' A11^{-1} (Lambda Z'X)
  y'Py = y'y - (Lambda Z'y)' A11^{-1} (Lambda Z'y) - rhs' beta_hat

Gradient of each term with respect to theta_k (using the matrix derivative identity d/dtheta log|A| = tr(A^{-1} dA/dtheta)):

  d/dtheta_k log|A11| = tr(A11^{-1} dA11/dtheta_k)

where dA11/dtheta_k = dLambda_k' Z'Z Lambda + Lambda' Z'Z dLambda_k (and dLambda_k is sparse — only the block for spec j changes).

For the diagonal (intercept-only) path, dLambda/dtheta_k = diag(e_k) (indicator for factor k), making dA11/dtheta_k block-structured and cheap to compute.

Implementation plan:
1. Add reml_gradient(theta, cache, specs, n_levels, q_sizes) -> np.ndarray
2. For the diagonal path: use tr(A11^{-1} * dA11_k) = sum of selected diagonal elements of A11^{-1}
3. For the general (slopes) path: use automatic differentiation via jax.grad or numerical fallback
4. Wire into fit_reml: pass jac=reml_gradient to opt.minimize when optimizer='lbfgsb'
5. Benchmark: compare eval counts and wall time on many_firms / large_scale fixtures

## Acceptance criteria
- reml_gradient matches finite-difference gradient to rtol=1e-4 on all fixtures
- L-BFGS-B eval count drops from ~65-75 to ~12-15 for intercept-only models
- fit_reml results (beta, theta, llf) unchanged to rtol=1e-6
- All existing profiled_reml tests pass
close_reason: Analytical REML gradient implemented and tested; wired into fit_reml via use_gradient=True

title: Structured summary() and VarCorr() output
description:
Implement a formatted summary() method and VarCorr() function matching lme4/lmerTest output style.

## Why

R users expect summary(model) to print a structured report with: model call, REML criterion, scaled residuals, random effects table (variance, SD, correlations), fixed effects table (estimate, SE, df, t, p), and correlation of fixed effects. Currently interlace has no summary() method — users must manually inspect individual attributes. This is the single most visible UX gap for R-world users.

## What needs to be done

### summary()
- CrossedLMEResult.summary() → a SummaryResult object with __repr__ that prints:
  - Model formula and fitting method
  - REML/ML criterion at convergence
  - Random effects table: group, name (Intercept/slope), Variance, Std.Dev., and correlation if applicable
  - Residual variance and SD
  - Number of obs, number of groups per factor
  - Fixed effects table: Estimate, Std.Error, (df if Satterthwaite implemented), t value, Pr(>|t|)
  - Convergence status

### VarCorr()
- Standalone VarCorr(result) function returning a structured object with .as_dataframe() showing variance components and correlations in lme4 VarCorr format.

## Acceptance criteria

- str(model.summary()) matches lme4 summary() layout for sleepstudy fixture (column names, numeric values to 4 sig figs).
- VarCorr(model).as_dataframe() has columns: grp, var1, var2, vcov, sdcor matching lme4 VarCorr output.

title: allFit(): multi-optimizer convergence check
description:
Implement allFit() to refit a model with all available optimizers and report convergence agreement.

## Why

lme4's allFit() is a practical safety net: it refits with Nelder-Mead, L-BFGS-B, BOBYQA, etc. and compares the resulting log-likelihoods and parameter estimates. When estimates disagree across optimizers it signals a flat likelihood surface, near-singular fit, or local optima — issues that a single optimizer silently masks. This is especially important in production pipelines like gpgap where convergence failures are hard to detect downstream.

## What needs to be done

- allFit(formula, data, ...) refits with each available optimizer (lbfgsb always; bobyqa if installed; add Nelder-Mead via scipy.optimize.minimize).
- Return an AllFitResult with: .results (dict optimizer_name → CrossedLMEResult), .converged (dict), .summary() table showing llf, theta, fe_params per optimizer, max pairwise diff.
- Flag when max pairwise diff in llf > 0.001 or in any theta > 1% as a 'possible convergence issue'.
- Parallel execution optional (map over optimizers).

## Acceptance criteria

- allFit() returns results for all installed optimizers without error.
- summary() table is human-readable and flags disagreement.
- A known flat-likelihood fixture (e.g., single group with few obs) triggers the convergence warning.
close_reason: Implemented allFit() with lbfgsb, nelder-mead, and optional bobyqa optimizers; AllFitResult with converged dict, possible_issue flag, and summary() table; 11 tests all pass

title: simulate() and parametric bootstrap (bootMer equivalent)
description:
Add the ability to simulate new response vectors from a fitted model, and use that to implement a parametric bootstrap for flexible CI/SE estimation.

## Why

lme4's simulate() and bootMer() are the most flexible inference tools for mixed models. Once you can draw from the fitted model, you can bootstrap CIs for any quantity: fixed effects, variance components, BLUPs, predictions, custom contrasts. This closes a significant gap for users who need inference beyond Wald approximations.

## What needs to be done

### simulate()
- Given a fitted CrossedLMEResult, draw nsim new response vectors from the conditional model:
    y* = X*beta + Z*u* + eps*, u* ~ N(0, G), eps* ~ N(0, sigma^2 * I)
- Return an (n, nsim) array or DataFrame of simulated responses.
- Support seed parameter for reproducibility.

### bootMer()
- Parametric bootstrap: for each of B iterations, simulate y* from fitted model, refit model on (X, Z, y*), collect statistic of interest.
- statistic callable: function(fitted_result) → scalar or array (default: collect theta + sigma + fe_params).
- Return a BootResult with .estimates (B x p array), .ci(method='perc'|'bca', level=0.95).
- Progress bar via tqdm (already a dependency).

## Acceptance criteria

- simulate(nsim=1000) produces samples with mean ≈ fitted values and variance ≈ sigma^2 + VC contributions.
- bootMer(B=200) CI for fixed effects contains lme4 point estimates in >90% of simulation studies.
- bootMer is seeded and reproducible.
close_reason: simulate() and bootMer() implemented with full test coverage

title: Profile likelihood confidence intervals for variance components
description:
Implement profile likelihood CIs for variance components (theta / sigma^2) as an alternative to Wald CIs.

## Why

Wald CIs for variance components are known to be unreliable, especially near the boundary (theta→0) and in small samples. lme4's confint(model, method='profile') traces the profile likelihood surface to get better-calibrated intervals. This is the recommended default in R for variance component CIs.

## What needs to be done

- For each variance parameter theta_i (and residual sigma), hold other params fixed at MLE and scan theta_i over a grid to trace the profile log-likelihood.
- Find the CI endpoints by interpolating where 2*(llf_max - llf(theta_i)) = qchisq(level, df=1).
- Expose as result.confint(method='profile', level=0.95) returning a DataFrame with columns: 2.5%, 97.5% for each VC param and for fixed effects (for FEs, profile CI is equivalent to Wald in linear case but include for completeness).
- The existing profiled_reml.py objective function can be reused directly — profiling is just 1D scans over theta.

## Acceptance criteria

- confint(method='profile') matches lme4 profile CIs to <5% relative error on sleepstudy fixture.
- Returns finite intervals (or [0, upper] when theta boundary is hit).
- confint(method='wald') still works and returns the existing Wald-based intervals.
close_reason: All 3 acceptance criteria met: (1) profile CIs match lme4 <5% on sleepstudy+dyestuff, (2) boundary case [0,upper] works, (3) confint(method='wald') returns Wald FE CIs

After the formula.py change, RandomEffectSpec objects for nested terms will have interaction_cols=['batch','cask'] but no actual 'batch:cask' column in the dataframe. The Z-matrix builder needs to synthesise this grouping factor from the component columns.

if spec.interaction_cols:

title: Extend RandomEffectSpec and parse_random_effects for / nesting
description:
Update src/interlace/formula.py to parse lme4-style nested random effect syntax (1|g1/g2) by expanding it into multiple RandomEffectSpec objects.

## Why

The formula parser currently only handles simple group names matching \w+. The / nesting shorthand is a direct analogue of lme4's expansion rule: (1|g1/g2) -> (1|g1) + (1|g1:g2). This step implements the parse-time expansion.

## What needs to be done

### 1. Add interaction_cols field to RandomEffectSpec

```python
@dataclass
class RandomEffectSpec:
    group: str                          # e.g. 'batch' or 'batch:cask'
    predictors: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    intercept: bool = True
    correlated: bool = True
    interaction_cols: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    # Non-empty means this group is a derived interaction of these columns.
    # e.g. interaction_cols=['batch','cask'] means group='batch:cask' is
    # constructed at Z-build time as str(batch) + ':' + str(cask).
```

### 2. Update the regex in parse_random_effects

The group capture group currently uses \w+ which does not match / characters. Change it to allow \w+(/\w+)* so that 'batch/cask' and 'batch/cask/sub' are captured.

### 3. Add expansion logic after regex match

After extracting the group string, check if it contains /. If it does:
- Split by / to get parts, e.g. ['batch', 'cask'] or ['a', 'b', 'c']
- Expand into multiple specs by building cumulative interaction prefixes:
  - depth 1: RandomEffectSpec(group='batch', intercept=<same as original>, predictors=<same>, correlated=<same>, interaction_cols=[])
  - depth 2: RandomEffectSpec(group='batch:cask', intercept=<same>, predictors=<same>, correlated=<same>, interaction_cols=['batch', 'cask'])
  - depth 3: RandomEffectSpec(group='a:b:c', intercept=<same>, predictors=<same>, correlated=<same>, interaction_cols=['a', 'b', 'c'])
- Return all specs from this single input string (the outer loop in parse_random_effects collects them all)

### 4. Update spec_to_str

When interaction_cols is non-empty, spec_to_str should reconstruct a meaningful string. The canonical form is '(1 | batch:cask)' (i.e. show the derived group name, not the / form). This is fine for repr purposes.

### 5. No changes needed to groups_to_random_effects

The groups= parameter shorthand only produces plain intercept specs; nesting via / is only available through the random= parameter.

## Acceptance criteria

- parse_random_effects(['(1|batch/cask)']) returns exactly 2 RandomEffectSpec objects
- First: group='batch', interaction_cols=[]
- Second: group='batch:cask', interaction_cols=['batch', 'cask']
- parse_random_effects(['(1|a/b/c)']) returns 3 specs
- parse_random_effects(['(1|g)']) behaviour unchanged
- All existing tests still pass (make test)

description: Read through residuals.py, leverage.py, influence.py, and augment.py and document every place that assumes scalar Lambda_theta, single-column-per-group Z, or intercept-only random effects structure. Produce a findings list as issue notes — this drives the scope of the subsequent fix tasks.
notes:
## Findings

### residuals.py
1. **hlm_resid level=group_name (L96-102)**: Assumes random_effects[level] is pd.Series — calls re_series.name, re_series.values, re_series.index. A DataFrame has .values and .index but not a single .name. Group-level residual output breaks for random-slopes groups.

### leverage.py
2. **_crossed_structures D matrix (L48-51)**: Builds D as blkdiag(var_j * eye(q_j)) for each group col, assuming variance_components[col] is a scalar. For random slopes it is a (p_j x p_j) DataFrame; D must instead be blkdiag(cov_j ⊗ I_{q_j}) (Kronecker-based block).
3. **_crossed_structures Zi construction (L62-70)**: Builds Zi with q_total columns, placing a single 1 per obs per factor (intercept-only pattern). For random slopes, each group factor contributes n_terms*q_j columns and Zi rows must include the predictor values for the slope terms, not just indicator bits.

### influence.py
4. **_full_params theta extraction (L41-44)**: Flattens variance_components into a 1-D numpy array. Fails when any VC is a DataFrame (random slopes). Theta must instead flatten cov_j into its lower-triangular Cholesky entries (like the REML theta parameterisation).
5. **_refit (L64-69)**: Always refits using groups= API (intercept-only). Loses random-slope structure entirely — the reduced model will be mis-specified.
6. **_refit_groups_arg (L103-108)**: Returns groups-only arg; no equivalent for random= specs with slopes.
7. **_reduced_params (L89-93)**: Same scalar VC assumption as _full_params.
8. **tau_gap (L404-406)**: np.sqrt(max(vc_full[factor], 0.0)) fails for DataFrame VCs; tau computation needs to use the diagonal of the cov matrix (marginal SDs per term) or a single summary scalar.

### augment.py
No direct intercept-only assumptions. Delegates entirely to hlm_resid and hlm_influence — will work once those are fixed.

### Root cause
The _gpgap_group_col + _gpgap_vc_cols + groups= refit pattern was designed for intercept-only models. The fix tasks need to:
- Store RandomEffectSpec list on CrossedLMEResult (or ModelInfo) so diagnostics can refit with the correct random= specs
- Rebuild D as blkdiag(sigma2 * L_j L_j' ⊗ I_{q_j}) for each spec
- Rebuild Zi with slope predictor values in the right columns
- Flatten/compare VCs consistently using the Cholesky theta parameterisation or diagonal SDs

title: Support Python 3.10-3.12 (currently pinned to >=3.13)
description:
## Motivation
`pyproject.toml` currently has `requires-python = \">=3.13\"`. Python 3.13 was released 2024-10; many ML/data-science projects in industry are still on 3.10 or 3.11 because their downstream stacks (PyTorch wheels, MLflow versions, internal platform images, AWS SageMaker base images, Kedro/Airflow versions) trail. Pinning to 3.13 makes interlace unusable as a drop-in dependency in those projects.

Concrete blocker: the Stepstone `salary-models` repo is pinned to Python 3.10 via Poetry (the `ai_project` Kedro project). Even with `family=\"student_t\"` and `dispformula` shipped, interlace cannot be added as a runtime dependency. The only workarounds are:
  - vendoring source (loses upgrade path), or
  - running interlace out-of-process from a separate 3.13 venv (operational overhead and serialisation friction)

Both are bad enough that the salary team will stay on Stan instead.

## Scope
Determine the *actual* hard floor by:
1. Auditing language features used in `src/interlace/`:
   - PEP 695 type parameter syntax (`type Foo = ...`, `class Foo[T]: ...`) — 3.12+
   - `typing.override` / `@override` decorator — 3.12+ (or `typing_extensions` backport for 3.10+)
   - `match` statements — 3.10+ (likely fine)
   - `str.removeprefix/removesuffix` etc. — already ≥3.9
   - f-string `=` debug — already ≥3.8
2. Auditing dependencies' floors (statsmodels, scipy, numpy, pandas, plotnine, scikit-sparse).
3. Picking a target floor — `>=3.10` would maximally unblock industry users; `>=3.11` if 3.10 audit reveals too much churn.

## Implementation notes
- Replace 3.12+ syntax with the equivalent older form (`TypeVar` instead of PEP 695, `typing_extensions.override` for 3.10/3.11).
- Add the lower-bounded Python versions to `pyproject.toml` `classifiers`.
- Extend CI matrix in `.github/workflows/` to test the supported floor.
- Update `installation.md` and any \"Requires Python ≥ 3.13\" mentions in `README.md` and `docs/`.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `requires-python` lowered to `>=3.10` (preferred) or at minimum `>=3.11`
- [ ] CI runs the test suite on each supported minor version
- [ ] README and installation docs updated
- [ ] No runtime regressions on 3.13 (existing tests still pass)
- [ ] If `scikit-sparse` (`[fast]` extra) requires a higher floor, document that the fast path has a stricter Python requirement than the slow path

## Out of scope
- Supporting Python <3.10 (3.9 is EOL Oct 2025, not worth the cost)
- Performance optimisations that would specifically benefit older interpreters

title: Last resort: Numba/Cython JIT for PIRLS inner kernel
description:
## Why
If after Tier 1-3 we are still >3x slower on CBPP, the remaining gap is
Python interpreter overhead in the PIRLS inner loop body (working
weights, working response, convergence check). Compiling that body
buys back most of the residual gap at the cost of:

  - Adding numba (or Cython) to deps -- breaks "pure-Python, scipy-only".
  - Wheel/install complexity (numba is heavy; Cython requires a
    compiler at sdist install time).

## What (only if needed)
  - Extract the PIRLS inner body in glmm_laplace._pirls into a pure
    NumPy function with no scipy.sparse touches (sparse solve stays
    outside the jit).
  - @numba.njit it; benchmark.

## Decision gate
Do NOT start until:
  - Profile (interlace-1yyz) confirms PIRLS Python overhead is the
    dominant remaining cost.
  - Tier 1-3 tasks are all closed.
  - Resulting CBPP ratio is still > 3x.

## Acceptance criteria
  - Bench on CBPP closes to within 2-3x.
  - Numba is gated as an optional [fast] extra; pure-Python path still
    works (just slower).

title: Cross-validation utilities with group-aware splits
description:
Add k-fold and leave-one-group-out (LOGO) cross-validation utilities that respect the grouped structure of mixed models.

## Why

Standard CV splits can leak group information across train/test sets in mixed models. Leave-one-group-out CV (analogous to lme4 community tools and caret's groupKFold) is the correct approach: hold out all observations for one group, refit on remaining data, predict for held-out group. This is essential for evaluating predictive performance and for model selection in the gpgap pipeline.

## What needs to be done

- cross_val(formula, data, groups, cv='logo'|'kfold', k=5, scoring='rmse'|'mae'|callable) function.
- LOGO: for each unique group value, train on all other groups, predict on held-out group using predict(newdata) with unseen-group shrinkage-to-zero behaviour.
- KFold: stratified k-fold that keeps groups intact (no observation-level splitting within a group).
- Returns a CVResult with per-fold scores, mean, SD, and optionally the per-fold fitted results.
- Progress bar via tqdm.

## Acceptance criteria

- LOGO CV on sleepstudy returns RMSE comparable to lme4-based LOGO benchmarks.
- KFold with groups='subject' never splits a subject across train/test folds.
- cross_val works with polars DataFrames via narwhals.

title: update() method for model refitting
description:
Add an update() method to CrossedLMEResult to refit with a modified formula or data, matching R's update.merMod().

## Why

update() is a core ergonomic feature of R's modelling ecosystem. Instead of calling fit() from scratch with a modified formula, users can do update(model, . ~ . + x2) or update(model, data=new_data). This is heavily used in model-building workflows and makes interlace feel native to R users.

## What needs to be done

- Implement CrossedLMEResult.update(formula=None, data=None, **kwargs) that:
  - Merges new formula/data/kwargs with original model spec stored in result.model.
  - Calls fit() with merged spec and returns a new CrossedLMEResult.
  - Supports lme4-style . notation (. ~ . + x means add x to existing fixed effects) — can use formulaic or simple string manipulation.
- Also expose as a module-level update(result, ...) function for consistency with statsmodels style.

## Acceptance criteria

- update(model, formula='. ~ . + x2') adds x2 to fixed effects and refits.
- update(model, data=new_df) refits on new data with same formula.
- update(model, method='ML') changes fitting method.
- Returned result is a valid CrossedLMEResult passing all existing result tests.
close_reason: Implemented CrossedLMEResult.update() and module-level update(); full lme4 dot notation support; all 16 new tests pass

title: Random effect prediction intervals (uncertainty around BLUPs)
description:
Add prediction intervals around BLUP estimates to quantify uncertainty in random effect estimates.

## Why

BLUPs (Best Linear Unbiased Predictors) are point estimates with associated uncertainty that is currently not exposed. R's merTools::predictInterval() and arm::se.ranef() provide SE and CI around BLUPs. Users interpreting random effects — e.g., school effects in education research, or firm effects in pay-gap analysis — need uncertainty bands, not just point estimates.

## What needs to be done

- Implement SE for BLUPs using the posterior variance formula:
    Var(u | y) = G - G*Z'*V⁻¹*Z*G  (conditional variance of random effects)
  This requires V⁻¹ which is already computed during the Cholesky solve.
- Add random_effects_se property on CrossedLMEResult: dict mapping group → Series of SEs.
- Add random_effects_ci(level=0.95) method returning symmetric normal-approximation CIs.
- Parametric bootstrap alternative: use bootMer() (once implemented) for more accurate intervals.

## Acceptance criteria

- random_effects_se values are positive and finite for all groups.
- CIs match arm::se.ranef() output to <10% relative error on sleepstudy fixture.
- Works for both random intercept and random slope models.
close_reason: Implemented random_effects_se property and random_effects_ci() method on CrossedLMEResult. Uses posterior variance formula Var(b|y) = σ² * Lambda * A11⁻¹ * Lambda'. All 15 new tests pass including analytical closed-form check on Dyestuff.

title: GLMM support: glmer() equivalent (Binomial, Poisson)
description:
Implement generalized linear mixed models (GLMM) with Laplace approximation, analogous to lme4::glmer().

## Why

lme4::glmer() is heavily used for binary and count outcomes (logistic mixed models, Poisson mixed models). interlace currently only handles Gaussian response. Closing this gap would make interlace applicable to a much wider range of problems — and is the single largest feature gap vs. lme4.

## What needs to be done

This is a large scope item. High-level plan:

### Phase 1: API and Laplace approximation
- Add family parameter to fit(): family='binomial'|'poisson'|'gaussian' (default).
- For non-Gaussian families, switch from profiled REML to penalized iteratively reweighted least squares (PIRLS) with Laplace approximation of the marginal likelihood.
- The Laplace approximation integrates out u using a quadratic approximation at the mode: log p(y|theta) ≈ log p(y|u_hat, theta) + log p(u_hat|theta) - 0.5*log|H|.

### Phase 2: Adaptive Gaussian quadrature (AGQ)
- More accurate than Laplace for small nq; lme4 uses nAGQ parameter.
- Implement AGQ as an optional refinement (nAGQ=1 = Laplace, nAGQ>1 = AGQ).

### Phase 3: Result compatibility
- GLMMResult that mirrors CrossedLMEResult attributes but adds link function, fitted on response scale, etc.

## Acceptance criteria

- glmer equivalent (fit(family='binomial')) matches lme4 glmer fixed effects to <0.01 on cbpp fixture.
- Converges for standard binomial and Poisson datasets.
- GLMMResult exposes fe_params, random_effects, predict() on both link and response scales.

## Notes

This is the highest-effort epic (Tier 3). Recommend tackling after Tier 1 and Tier 2 epics are complete.
close_reason: Phase 1 complete: GLMMFamily protocol, Laplace/PIRLS estimation, glmer() public API, and predict(). All acceptance criteria met. AGQ (Phase 2) can be a separate epic.

title: Add dynamic versioning with setuptools-scm
description:
## Why

Version is currently hardcoded as a static string in pyproject.toml. As we approach proper releases, this is error-prone — it's easy to forget to bump the version before tagging.

setuptools-scm derives the package version automatically from git tags (e.g. v0.1.0), eliminating manual version bumps entirely.

## What needs to be done

1. Add setuptools-scm to the build-system requires in pyproject.toml
2. Change version from static to dynamic field:
   - Remove: `version = "0.1.0"`
   - Add: `dynamic = ['version']`
3. Add tool config section:
   ```toml
   [tool.setuptools_scm]
   version_scheme = 'no-guess-dev'
   local_scheme = 'no-local-version'
   version_file = 'src/interlace/_version.py'
   ```
4. Add src/interlace/_version.py to .gitignore (it is generated at build time)
5. Ensure a git tag matching v0.1.0 (or 0.1.0) exists before building

## Acceptance criteria

- `uv build` succeeds and the wheel filename reflects the correct version from the latest git tag
- `make check` still passes
- No static version string remains in pyproject.toml
close_reason: hatch-vcs added; version derived from git tags; no static version in pyproject.toml; uv build produces correctly-versioned wheel
